# Unit F, phase 1: the new text's assertions, one per sentence

### 12.5 Scripts and the mid-run mutation doctrine
- V1 This section settles what the periphery (everything outside the loop that exchanges data with it) may do to a running model.
- V2 The periphery's attached participants are its devices.
- V3 The section surveys FlightCore's mid-run mutations, states the clock criterion that maps scripts to components (units of modeling), eliminates `user_callback!`, covers manual events and mid-run re-initialization, and ends with the doctrine's final form.
- V4 What the consumers demonstrably mutate mid-run is surveyed here.
- V5 The line references are to `c172_demos.jl`, FlightCore's demo file.
- V6 FlightCore's `user_callback!` has exactly two archetypes.
- V7 The first is the timetable script, `elevator_offset` as a function of `t` (c172_demos.jl:290).
- V8 The second is the synthetic pilot, a phase FSM (finite-state machine) reading `y` and writing mode requests, references, flaps and wind (c172_demos.jl:423, 525).
- V9 Both write only `u` fields.
- V10 No demo, test or GUI path pokes `x`/`s` mid-run, and `init!`/trim appear only between construction and `run!` (c172_demos.jl:303).
- V11 A sim-time script becomes a scenario component, and a wall-clock interaction becomes a device (D-031). [D-031] (bold)
- V12 A scenario component is an ordinary periodic discrete component holding a sim-time script.
- V13 Sim-time scripts are model behavior, which is why they become scenario components.
- V14 Both archetypes are clocked by sim time, `t`, the trajectory.
- V15 Mapping them to devices is rejected (D-031). [D-031]
- V16 The clock is the criterion.
- V17 A script mapped to a component is periodic discrete, with `K = 1` for the `dt = 0.02` callbacks FlightCore had, `K` being the multiplier in `Relative(K)` (§10.5). [§10.5]
- V18 It executes synchronously in the loop, deterministic paced or unpaced.
- V19 It is replayed by recomputation, with no trace (the records of each frame's drained inputs).
- V20 A device, by contrast, is traced and replayed from the trace.
- V21 The component mapping is strictly richer than the callback it replaces.
- V22 The callback's `Ref(:init)` phase closure becomes honest `s`, which a port (one declared name with its cell) can publish to snapshots, logs and plots.
- V23 A snapshot is the immutable per-boundary publication.
- V24 Inputs arrive same-boundary (a published consistency point) fresh by topological order.
- V25 The callback ran post-step, one boundary staler.
- V26 The pure timetable script is a one-liner reading the clock out of its bundle (the NamedTuple of zero-copy views a component function receives).
- V27 That one-liner is `y_direct(c, (; t)) = (; offset = profile(t))`, exact at its own ticks, with no latch state of its own.
- V28 A tick is an instant at which a discrete component's stages and update run.
- V29 In a scenario configuration the script drives the input ports of the avionics (the onboard flight systems).
- V30 §11.7 therefore renders the corresponding GUI widgets read-only with its source shown. [§11.7]
- V31 The port-resolution rule resolves FlightCore's demo-vs-GUI dead-slider fight (§11.7). [§11.7]
- V32 `user_callback!` is eliminated (D-031). [D-031] (bold)
- V33 It is the periphery's `f_step!`, FlightCore's unconditional per-step hook (§2.5), and cheap composition leaves it without justification. [§2.5]
- V34 Its call sites migrate to scenario components, not devices.
- V35 Manual event triggering needs no mechanism (D-031). [D-031] (bold)
- V36 It takes a root input (the root component's own input face) plus a boundary-detected guard (an edge check at step boundaries only, with no root-finding) reading that root input.
- V37 That is already expressible in settled machinery.
- V38 The levels doctrine applies (§11.4), with latched commands or counters. [§11.4]
- V39 The engine start/stop buttons of FlightCore's demos were `u`-writes.
- V40 Mid-run re-initialization is not built (D-031), because it is not demonstrated. [D-031] (bold)
- V41 Initialization and trim are stopped-sim workflows (first-class services, §14). [§14]
- V42 No concurrency perimeter exists there.
- V43 There is no loop and no devices, just plain single-task code.
- V44 The shape of the guarded addition (a capability the design admits but does not build) is on record should demand appear.
- V45 It would be a traced, boundary-executed intervention command applied through project → sweep → publish, so that no consumer ever observes un-decoded state.
- V46 In the doctrine's final form, while a simulation runs, the periphery stages root-input writes and issues control commands (§2.2, D-031). [§2.2, D-031] (bold)
- V47 Structurally, it does nothing else.
- V48 Anything that wants to poke the model mid-run is one of three things.
- V49 It is an input in disguise, so wire a root input and a guard.
- V50 It is model behavior in disguise, so add a scenario component.
- V51 It is a wall-clock interaction, so attach a device.
- V52 Graceful termination follows the same shape (§13.5). [§13.5]
- V53 It is a stop request (an output port of the framework enum `StopFlag`) declared in the model, honoured unless the advance ignores it (D-316). [D-316]
- V54 It is never a callback, and never a thrown exception (D-060). [D-060]

### 12.6 Run lifecycle and partial advance
- V55 This section specifies what a `Simulation` and its run own, the lifecycle a simulation moves through, how it advances and restarts, and what it keeps of its devices (any attached participants in the periphery) across runs.
- V56 A simulation is in one of five lifecycle states, built, initialized, running, stopped or errored.
- V57 A door is an entry point that builds a run, and there are three, `init!`, `restore!` and `replay!`.
- V58 A run's `feed` is the recording `replay!` attached, or `nothing`.
- V59 The input mode says where the next frame (one grid step, the unit of scheduling) takes its inputs from.
- V60 In `:live` they come from the staging cells (where each device's pending batch waits between drains), and in `:replay` from the attached recording.

#### The run and the simulation
- V61 `Run` is what one run owns (D-255, D-260, D-317). [D-255, D-260, D-317] (bold)
- V62 It is a mutable struct of six fields.
- V63 Two are `const` and last the run's whole life.
- V64 One is the log (the retained sequence of published snapshots).
- V65 The other is the trace (the records of each frame's drained inputs), which is `nothing` under the trace switch.
- V66 The door that builds the run takes the four recording keywords, `trace`, `log`, `log_every` and `log_max` (Appendix B, D-261). [Appendix B, D-261]
- V67 A run's recording is therefore that door's declaration, and the next door may declare otherwise (D-261). [D-261]
- V68 Four fields evolve during the run.
- V69 `feed` is the recording `replay!` attached, or `nothing`.
- V70 `termination` is the record the loop's tail writes.
- V71 `frame` and `boundary` are the trajectory's counters, the frame index and the boundary ordinal.
- V72 `init!`, `restore!` and `replay!` construct a run, and nothing else rebinds it.
- V73 `live!` (§12.7) and the halt at a recording's end write `feed`. [§12.7]
- V74 The loop's tail writes `termination` once, and `closed(run)` is `termination !== nothing`.
- V75 Each door sets the two counters as it builds the run, `init!` to zero and `restore!` and `replay!` to the checkpoint's, and the loop advances them (D-317). [D-317]
- V76 `restore!` of a bare state sets the frame index to the state's frame and the boundary ordinal to zero, as `init!` does (D-319). [D-319]
- V77 The origin `t₀` is not a run field (D-260). [D-260]
- V78 The executor's clock holds it beside `t`.
- V79 `init!` sets it on the clock before boundary zero, the initialization boundary (§14.5). [§14.5]
- V80 A checkpoint (the `Model`'s state at a frame top as one value) carries it with the clock (§11.5, D-273). [§11.5, D-273]
- V81 It is a `Float64`, as `h` and `t_end` are (D-260). [D-260]
- V82 A `Simulation` is constructed with a placeholder run (D-255). [D-255] (bold)
- V83 The placeholder is an empty log, no trace, no feed and no termination, and `init!`, `restore!` and `replay!` replace it (D-255). [D-255]
- V84 The field is always a `Run` and never `nothing`, so every accessor has a run to read, and the lifecycle state below says whether that run ever started.
- V85 The placeholder carries no configuration and no compiled state (D-261). [D-261]
- V86 `init!` allocates fresh objects rather than clearing them (D-255). [D-255]
- V87 `Simulation` is a mutable struct of four fields, the `Model` (the deployment and its executor at one scalar), the run, the data plane and the control plane (D-317). [D-317] (bold)
- V88 The control plane is the atomic surface carrying pause, pace and stop.
- V89 The `Model` holds the deployment, the executor, its status and its diagnostic cell.
- V90 The deployment is the scalar-free artifact the grid parameters fix, carrying the build.
- V91 The executor is the compiled form of the stage execution order, and a diagnostic cell is a writer's own holding place for runtime diagnostics.
- V92 A simulation owns its `Model`, claimed at construction and never shared (§9.2, D-318). [§9.2, D-318]
- V93 Every other value belongs to one of the four (D-256). [D-256]
- V94 The build is reached through the deployment, never held twice.
- V95 The grid parameters, the schedule (the typed per-component `(D, Φ, Δt)` tick table) and the event parameters are the deployment's (§9.2). [§9.2]
- V96 `chunk_size`, the stepper and the arrival buffers are the executor's.
- V97 `join_timeout` is `Control`'s (§12.1). [§12.1]
- V98 The loop's diagnostic cell, its account and the published holder are the plane's, and the frame's own cell is the `Model`'s (§11.8). [§11.8]
- V99 The log, the trace and the two counters are the run's.
- V100 The stop policy, with its `t_end` and ignored requesters, is the advance's argument, and the termination record (the stopped-sim value naming how the run ended) keeps the terminating one (D-260). [D-260]
- V101 The pacer's schedule and counters are `run!`'s own, created per call and passed to the loop and its publications as the policy is.
- V102 The status of each snapshot (the immutable per-boundary publication) carries their frozen record (§10.7, D-269). [§10.7, D-269]
- V103 A struct holds what it owns or what it must retain across calls (D-261). [D-261] (bold)
- V104 A callee takes what it reads as an argument, never off a field added to the container it already holds.
- V105 An object is built after its inputs exist, and the placeholder run above is the one exception (D-261). [D-261] (bold)

#### Lifecycle states and the input mode
- V106 A `Simulation` moves through five states, built, initialized, running, and terminally stopped or errored (§13.4, D-088). [§13.4, D-088] (bold)
- V107 Built means stores (the framework-owned homes of a component's state) allocated and boundary zero not completed (D-223). [D-223]
- V108 It is the cold state, and the state a throw inside boundary zero returns the simulation to (§13.4). [§13.4]
- V109 Initialized means `init!` has completed boundary zero, the initialization boundary run as the ordinary macro-sequence with an empty integrate (§14.5), or `restore!` or `replay!` has restored a checkpoint. [§14.5]
- V110 `lifecycle(sim)` derives the state rather than storing it (D-317). [D-317] (bold)
- V111 It reads three facts, the control plane's running flag, the `Model`'s status and whether the run is closed.
- V112 The status is `:built`, `:consistent` or `:inconsistent`, and only the `Model`'s own entry points and catch sites write it.
- V113 A claimed model's status is written only through its simulation's entry points, since the model's entry points refuse a direct call on a claimed model (D-318). [D-318]
- V114 set
- V115 any
- V116 any
- V117 running
- V118 clear
- V119 `:built`
- V120 any
- V121 built
- V122 clear
- V123 `:inconsistent`
- V124 any
- V125 errored
- V126 clear
- V127 `:consistent`
- V128 no
- V129 initialized
- V130 clear
- V131 `:consistent`
- V132 yes
- V133 stopped
- V134 `errored` is terminal (D-059). [D-059] (bold)
- V135 Reproduction is trace replay, not resurrection (§12.7). [§12.7]
- V136 Replay is the ordinary loop re-driven from the trace.
- V137 Beside the state, the run carries an input mode, `:live` or `:replay`, read as `mode(sim)`.
- V138 The mode is read off the run's `feed`, `:replay` while a recording is attached and `:live` otherwise (D-260). [D-260] (bold)
- V139 The mode names where the next frame's drain takes its batches from, the staging cells or the attached recording (§12.7, D-218). [§12.7, D-218]
- V140 The drain is the frame-top swap that publishes staged device writes into the root inputs, and a batch is a device's staged set of writes.
- V141 State and mode are orthogonal.
- V142 The state says whether the simulation may advance, and the mode says what it will advance on.
- V143 `init!` is mandatory (D-088). [D-088] (bold)
- V144 `run!` or `step!` on a simulation whose boundary zero has not completed is `MissingInit`, an error in the kind set (§13.2) naming `init!`. [§13.2]
- V145 That is distinct from `UninitializedInputs`, which fires inside `init!` (§14.6). [§14.6]
- V146 `restore!` and `replay!` are the two alternative doors.
- V147 Each restores a checkpoint and runs no boundary zero (§12.7, D-274). [§12.7, D-274]
- V148 A throw inside boundary zero, which only `init!` runs, leaves the simulation `built` (§13.4, D-223), so the next `run!` or `step!` meets the same refusal. [§13.4, D-223]

#### Partial advance
- V149 Deviceless, `run!` is fully synchronous, and §11.1 says where the loop and the device tasks run and defines the unattended run (a run with empty staging and no snapshot readers). [§11.1]
- V150 `step!(sim; frames = 1)` advances whole frames synchronously through the ordinary frame sequence (drain, integrate, boundaries, publication) and returns (D-088). [D-088]
- V151 A stepped simulation is bit-identical to the same frames under `run!` (§2.4), and it never waits on the pacer, whatever pace the control plane holds (D-269). [§2.4, D-269]
- V152 `step!(sim; t_plus = 10.0)` is the duration spelling.
- V153 It is mutually exclusive with `frames`, and passing both is `ArgumentInvalid`.
- V154 It advances whole frames until the boundary time first covers the duration, which is the migration suite's advance-by-duration idiom.
- V155 Partial advance is the test-harness mode of advance, assert, advance.
- V156 It is equally the REPL mode of fly a while, inspect, continue.
- V157 Neither is a script, so the scenario-component doctrine does not absorb them (§12.5). [§12.5]
- V158 A stepping session is deviceless by construction (D-093). [D-093] (bold)
- V159 Device tasks are per-`run!` artifacts (§11.1), and a device loop's `while running(handle)` is false outside a run. [§11.1]
- V160 Between `step!` calls the simulation is in a stopped-sim state, `initialized` (below), so `attach!` is legal there and does what it always does.
- V161 It registers (§11.3), and the task appears at the next `run!`. [§11.3]
- V162 The frame-top drain still runs, so `step!` frames stay bit-identical to `run!` frames.
- V163 In a stepping session the cell written is the harness cell (the always-present staging cell of the harness writer).
- V164 The harness write path is `stage!(sim, "face" => value, …)`, and §11.3 specifies that harness writer. [§11.3]
- V165 Staged batches are ordinary batches.
- V166 They are traced, so replay and bit-identity hold, and they are applied at the next frame top.
- V167 The read half is `latest(sim)`.
- V168 It hands back the same immutable snapshot value a device handle acquires (§11.2), navigated directly for assertions. [§11.2]
- V169 Advance-assert-advance is `stage!` → `step!` → `latest` (D-096). [D-096]
- V170 Both entry points work under `run!` too.
- V171 The harness cell is not step-scoped.
- V172 An inspection accessor leaves the rejection of closure-based termination untouched (§13.5, D-096). [§13.5, D-096]

#### Status, termination and `run!` after `step!`
- V173 Between `step!` calls a simulation reports `initialized` (D-088). [D-088]
- V174 No loop task exists, so `running` would lie.
- V175 Nothing is terminal, so `stopped` would lie too.
- V176 The state reads "boundary-consistent and ready to advance", not "sitting at boundary zero".
- V177 `run!` may therefore follow `step!`, continuing from the current boundary, and so may another `step!`.
- V178 Termination policy is honored throughout, as bit-identity requires.
- V179 `t_end` reached, or a stop request (an output port of the framework enum `StopFlag`) holding at frame 3 of `step!(sim; frames = 10)`, ends the run there through the ordinary §12.4 tail and leaves the simulation `stopped`. [§12.4]
- V180 `step!` therefore returns the number of frames actually advanced.
- V181 That is the requested count in the ordinary case, and fewer when the run terminated inside the call.
- V182 That return is how a harness detects the truncation without inspecting the clock.

#### Re-running and checkpoints
- V183 `stopped → init! → run!` remains the authored re-run (D-088). [D-088] (bold)
- V184 `init!` re-runs boundary zero from its condition (a path-addressed overlay that sets the build to a state).
- V185 The warm restart is `checkpoint` → `restore!` → `run!` (§12.7, D-274). [§12.7, D-274]
- V186 `restore!` is a door like `init!`, and it runs no boundary zero.
- V187 Each builds a fresh run, so the trace, the log and the termination record (§13.5) are new objects rather than cleared ones, and each clears any batches still in staging cells. [§13.5]
- V188 The recorders (the trace and the log jointly) restart with the run they record, and no stale batch survives to clobber the frame it predates.
- V189 `init!` and `restore!` also return the input mode to `:live`, and a fresh `replay!` sets the mode exactly as it sets the trajectory.
- V190 `live!` is the one call that moves the mode alone.
- V191 It takes a replaying simulation live where it stands (§12.7). [§12.7]
- V192 A terminal state makes the mode moot.
- V193 From `stopped`, nothing advances until `init!`, `restore!` or `replay!` opens a new run, and `errored` is terminal (D-218, D-219). [D-218, D-219]
- V194 `checkpoint` and `restore!` exist on the `Model` and on the `Simulation`, and a `Checkpoint` is the `Model`'s state beside the run's cursor (D-319). [D-319] (bold)
- V195 `checkpoint(model)` returns the state alone, a `ModelState`.
- V196 It holds the flat buffer, the `s` and `m` stores, the whole signal table, the guard priors, `t`, `t₀`, the fingerprint (the structural layout) and the deployment.
- V197 It is legal at `:consistent` with the clock on a grid top.
- V198 `checkpoint(sim)` wraps that state with the run's frame index and boundary ordinal (D-319). [D-319]
- V199 It is a stopped-sim service, legal in `initialized` and `stopped` (§14), and refused as `ServiceLifecycle` in any other state. [§14]
- V200 It is refused wherever the executor is not at the rest a published frame top leaves (`CheckpointMidFrame`, Appendix C). [Appendix C]
- V201 That is after a `t` stop, which leaves the clock mid-frame with the remainder abandoned, and after a frame abandoned unpublished (§12.4). [§12.4]
- V202 The test is that the clock sits on a grid time and that the latest snapshot is of that very boundary.
- V203 `restore!(model, model_state)` checks the state's fingerprint and deployment against the model.
- V204 It also checks that the state's `t` is a grid time `t₀ + k·h` of the state's own origin and step, and a state off its grid is `CheckpointMidFrame`.
- V205 Every mismatch of either kind is collected into one throw before any write.
- V206 The entry point then copies the state back, settles the restored boundary through the hooks and writes `:consistent` last (D-318, D-319). [D-318, D-319]
- V207 `restore!(sim, cp)` takes the four recording keywords `init!` takes.
- V208 It checks the state's fingerprint and deployment against the simulation as replay checks the trace header (the trace's fixed preamble), and a mismatch is `CheckpointMismatch` (§12.7). [§12.7]
- V209 It checks the state's `t` against its grid as the model's entry point does, collecting both kinds into one throw.
- V210 It then copies the state back, opens a fresh run with the checkpoint as its trace header, and publishes one snapshot at the checkpoint's `t`.
- V211 It runs no sweep, evaluates no guard, runs no update and resets no prior.
- V212 The next frame is the original lattice's next frame, because the clock came with the checkpoint.
- V213 The boundary ordinal continues, being the trajectory's (§12.3, D-274). [§12.3, D-274]
- V214 The snapshot `restore!` publishes is a re-publication.
- V215 It carries the ordinal of the boundary the checkpoint was taken at, and the next frame publishes under the next ordinal, as it did in the original run.
- V216 `restore!(sim, model_state)` is the door a state prepared on a standalone model takes into a simulation (§9.2, D-319). [§9.2, D-319]
- V217 It takes the same keywords and makes the same check of the state's fingerprint and deployment, and it refuses a state whose `t` is off the grid as `CheckpointMidFrame`.
- V218 It opens a fresh trajectory at the state's frame, and the restored boundary publishes under ordinal 0, as boundary zero's does.
- V219 A standalone model published nothing, so the trajectory has no ordinals to continue.
- V220 A `Checkpoint` holds a `ModelState{Float64}`, so it is nominal by type.
- V221 A state taken at another scalar is refused by dispatch with the same `CheckpointMismatch`, on either `restore!` that takes a bare state.

#### Device attachments across runs
- V222 Device attachments persist across re-initialization (D-088), because attachment is orthogonal to the run lifecycle (§11.3). [D-088, §11.3] (bold)
- V223 Persistence means roster persistence, the roster being the list of attached device entries.
- V224 Binding, claims (the set of faces a device may write) and device id survive.
- V225 Tasks and OS resources do not, the per-run topology being specified in §11.1 and the teardown in §12.4. [§11.1, §12.4]
- V226 Each `run!` re-initializes every rostered device and spawns its task (D-093). [D-093]
- V227 `attach!` while stopped only registers, and the task appears at the next `run!`.
- V228 Which devices get a task at each `run!` is decided as §11.1 specifies. [§11.1]
- V229 A front end attached by hand is still rostered (D-310), so the next `run!` spawns its task again. [D-310] (bold)

#### The stop policy per advance
- V230 The stop policy is declared per advance (D-255, D-316). [D-255, D-316] (bold)
- V231 `t_end` and `ignore_stop_requests` are keywords of `run!`, `replay!` and `step!`.
- V232 Each call builds and validates the `StopPolicy` (the immutable value of `t_end` plus the ignored requester paths) it passes to the loop (§13.5, D-255, D-316). [§13.5, D-255, D-316]
- V233 The value lives as long as the call, and afterwards only on the termination record of the advance that ended the run (D-260). [D-260]
- V234 A second run, or a `step!` sequence between two runs, can therefore stop on a different clock or honour a different set of stop requests without a rebuild.
